what_it_does: Printed electronics are circuits made with inkjet-style printing rather than silicon chip fabrication — they are cheap, flexible, and can be embedded in everyday objects, but they can only draw power from small printed batteries or energy-harvesting patches, so the total power budget is extremely tight. This paper looks at printed neuromorphic circuits (pNCs) — brain-inspired printed circuits that mimic how neurons fire — and asks how to train such a circuit to do a useful task while guaranteeing it stays within a hard power limit. Traditional approaches explore power-accuracy trade-offs by running hundreds of separate training experiments with different penalty weights, which is slow. The authors instead use a mathematical technique called Augmented Lagrangian optimization, which enforces the power constraint as a hard rule inside a single training run, automatically finding the best accuracy the circuit can achieve without ever exceeding the allowed power. The approach was tested on 13 different benchmark tasks, suggesting it generalizes across problem types, though specific accuracy numbers and power budgets are not confirmed from the abstract alone.
